1.pericope_label: The muster of the Kohathites, thirty to fifty

schools.summary: Gill places the second muster after the exchange of the firstborn, its object being to pick out those fit for service; Calvin gives the reason for a second count as the equal distribution of the charges, and argues the thirty-year floor from the levity of youth, which would detract from the reverence due to sacred things, and the fifty-year ceiling from the sloth that accompanies old age — a stricter rule than soldiering because religion is more precious than any earthly business.

Henry makes the ages a rule for ministry: God's service requires the best of our strength and the prime of our time, a man may make a good soldier much sooner than a good minister, ministers must not be novices and must learn before they teach; the release at fifty is a double kindness to the men and to the work, and those who put off repentance to old age leave the best work to the worst time.

Wesley makes thirty the age of full bodily strength and mature judgment together, noting that John and Christ alike began their ministry then; Clarke treats the varying ages — thirty here, twenty-five and twenty elsewhere — as a discrepancy to be reconciled, and begins from the exceeding severity of the Levitical service at this period.

Ellicott explains the precedence of the Kohathites by Moses and Aaron belonging to that family and by their office of bearing the ark, and contrasts the earlier Levite census from a month old with this one, aimed at duties requiring considerable physical strength; Keil and Delitzsch describe the procedure as raising them out of the sum total of the Levites, numbered first and separately.

debates: Whether the differing ages given for entering Levitical service (thirty here, twenty-five in Numbers 8, twenty in Chronicles) are a textual and historical problem to be reconciled, as Clarke takes them, or a graded apprenticeship in which the earlier ages mark probation and the later full service, as Henry reads them.

4.pericope_label: The priests cover the ark and the table

schools.summary: Calvin explains the assignment of offices from what men do when left to themselves — promiscuous sedulity begets confusion and ambition breeds quarrels — and narrows the Kohathite charge sharply: they were not to handle any part of the sanctuary but only to carry its vessels once the priests had packed them, the priests being warned that anything left uncovered would destroy their brethren; Gill distinguishes the badgers' skins here from the Gershonite covering of the tabernacle, made on purpose to keep off rain and dust and laid over the other coverings so as to preserve the veil as well.

Henry reads the covering itself as doctrine: the holy things were veiled not only for security and respect but to keep them from being seen, which marked both the reverence due them and the darkness of a dispensation whose types were still unopened — whereas now, through Christ, we are encouraged to come boldly to the throne of grace.

Wesley allows that on this necessary occasion the inferior priests were permitted into the holy of holies, identifies the covering veil as the second veil under which the ark stood, gives the reason for the wrapping as keeping the Levites from seeing or touching the ark, and presses the practical difficulty that corn had to be reserved in the wilderness for the weekly baking of the shewbread.

Ellicott suggests the entry was no violation because at the moving of the camp the Divine Presence seems to have departed from the Holy of Holies and ascended in the cloud, corrects the covering vail to the vail of the hanging and covers to cover withal to the cups of the drink-offering, and notes that the staves were withdrawn only while the covering went on; Keil and Delitzsch set out the exact order of cloths, vessels, bread, skin and bearing poles for the table of shewbread.

debates: Why the ordinary bar on entering the most holy place did not apply: Wesley treats it as a simple exception granted for the necessity of the march, while Ellicott argues there was nothing to violate, the Divine Presence having already withdrawn into the cloud.

9.pericope_label: The candlestick, the altars and the vessels covered

schools.summary: Gill finds a scale of sanctity in the number of wrappings — three coverings for the ark and the shewbread table, only two for the candlestick — explains the golden altar by its overlay of gold, marks the move outdoors to the court where the altar of burnt offering stood, and argues that the fire, though unmentioned, was doubtless preserved and carried with the altar or in a separate vessel, reporting Bishop Patrick's guess that it went upon the grate.

Wesley takes the instruments of ministry for the sacred garments and gathers the purpose of all the coverings under three heads — safety from rain and sun, decency in the blue and purple and scarlet, and concealment, a fit sign of the darkness of that dispensation, now that Christ has destroyed the face of the covering — and infers from the removal of the ashes alone that the heaven-kindled fire was kept burning in some vessel.

Ellicott corrects the bar to a pole or bearing frame and the censers to fire-pans, and recalls the earlier order to make pans for the ashes; Keil and Delitzsch list the candlestick's furniture and its two wrappings, describe the altar of incense laid on its frame, give the sequence for the brazen altar, and note that the copper laver is nowhere mentioned, probably because it was carried uncovered, dismissing the Greek and Samaritan supplement as a spurious interpolation.

15.pericope_label: The Kohathites bear; the charge of Eleazar

schools.summary: Gill will not let the word sanctuary stand loosely: what Aaron and his sons had made an end of covering was not the holy place nor the most holy place, since neither was covered by them, but the holy things within — the ark, the shewbread table and all that appertained to them — and he reports Jarchi's narrower reading of the holiness as the ark and the altar.

Wesley supplies the manner and the later history — the burden went on their shoulders, and in time the priests themselves, once multiplied, took these things up without excluding the Levites — and reads the prohibition exactly, that they were not to touch the holy things before those were covered; on Eleazar he takes the charge literally, that he himself was to carry these things and not commit them to the sons of Kohath.

Ellicott declines to emend the Hebrew from the Greek and Samaritan clause about the laver, thinking it more probable the laver simply went uncovered, marks the sharp line between the priests' work of dismantling and the Levites' work of moving, and presses the threat home through Uzzah, most probably a Kohathite, who of all men ought to have known the law; Keil and Delitzsch make Eleazar's charge supervisory, belonging to him as head of all the Levites and extending, as the later verses show, to the Kohathite services themselves.

debates: What Eleazar's charge amounted to: Wesley takes the oil, incense, meat-offering and anointing oil as things he was to carry with his own hands rather than commit to the Kohathites, while Keil and Delitzsch read the whole clause as an oversight belonging to him as head of all the Levites.

Whether the Hebrew is defective where the laver goes unmentioned: the Greek and Samaritan copies supply a clause for covering and carrying it, but Ellicott finds no sufficient ground for the addition and prefers to suppose the laver was transported uncovered.

17.pericope_label: Cut ye not off the Kohathites

schools.summary: Gill calls this a very solemn and awful charge given because the employment was hazardous, collects the Jewish softenings of the idiom — the Targum of Jonathan's give no occasion and Jarchi's be not the cause of their cutting off through negligence in the packing — and reads the exclusion of the Levites during the packing as a figure of the mysteries of grace lying hidden under the former dispensation.

Wesley states the warning as an appeal to God's justice rather than the priests' hands, that they should not by their neglect provoke God to cut the Kohathites off, and finds significance in every man being appointed to his own service and burden, the loads being equally distributed; Clarke keeps the literal image of swallowing down, reading it of the promptitude with which the holy things were put out of sight, without which reverence they could not have represented heavenly realities.

Keil and Delitzsch explain the repeated command as precaution against calamity, gloss the imperative as a warning against the priests' own mistake and negligence, take the word for tribe in its original sense of a stock, derive the disputed clause from swallowing as a proverbial phrase for a single instant, and defend the four verses against Knobel's charge of interpolation; Ellicott renders it for a moment, notes the peculiar use of tribe for one division of Levi, and defends the harsh phrasing on the principle that men may be said to do what their negligence brings about, as Paul writes destroy not him with thy meat for whom Christ died.

debates: What the disputed word governing the covering means: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott read it as a proverbial expression for a single instant, so that the Levites were not to look even for a moment, while Clarke keeps the literal sense of being swallowed down and takes it of the speed with which the holy things were put out of sight.
outliers: Knobel held that these four verses were interpolated by a later hand into the original text; Keil and Delitzsch answer that the linguistic grounds offered — the peculiar use of the word for tribe, the construction of the verb for approaching, and the causative form of the verb for cutting off — are weak throughout.

schools.summary: Calvin calls the Gershonite and Merarite tasks apparently mean and laborious, even servile, and draws from that the rule that in God's service nothing is to be despised, since it ought abundantly to satisfy us that God has deigned to choose us as ministers of his sanctuary, so that neither weariness nor pride should hinder us; Gill notes that Aaron shared in the muster though unnamed, that Gershon's seniority did not excuse his posterity, and divides the commission on Aben Ezra's lines between settled service and the burdens of the march.

Henry frames the two remaining families by comparison — their charge less honourable than the first but necessary and to be done regularly — describes the drapery taken down at the cloud's removal and set up again where it rested, notes that each man had his own piece so that none should be confused, is struck that thousands were employed where far fewer would have sufficed because the work had to be done with expedition, and observes that their own tents go unmentioned since God's house must be preferred before our own.

Wesley identifies the first item as the covering of goats' hair and the second as the ten curtains that covered the boards, the boards themselves going to the Merarites, places the rams' skins next above those curtains, and notes that the court compassed both the tabernacle and the altar.

Ellicott distinguishes the dwelling from the tent that covered it and holds the curtains of the dwelling to constitute the dwelling itself, the woodwork being subsidiary, so that the fine twined linen comes first and the goats' hair belongs to the tent; he prefers the tent of meeting to the tabernacle of the congregation and the hanging for the entrance to the hanging for the door, and observes that the court hangings enclosed the whole; Keil and Delitzsch note that the section is introduced exactly as the Kohathite one was.

debates: Which curtains the Gershonites bore first: Ellicott takes the opening word for the fine twined linen curtains of the dwelling, holding the woodwork subsidiary to them, while Wesley takes it for the goats' hair covering and assigns the ten linen curtains to the second phrase.

28.pericope_label: Ithamar’s oversight and the charge of the Merarites

schools.summary: Gill introduces Merari as Levi's third and youngest son, records without concealment that the Greek version reads twenty-five years old here and in the parallel place, reconciling it with the Hebrew by making twenty-five the age at which the Levites entered the tabernacle to wait and learn their business and thirty the age at which they entered upon it, and identifies the families concerned as the Mahlites and the Mushites.

Wesley reads the charge as being under Ithamar's conduct and direction, and turns the command to reckon the Merarite gear into an inventory, giving three reasons why a naming by name is required here and not before — these things were far more numerous, being meaner they might otherwise have been neglected, and the requirement teaches that God esteems nothing small in his service and expects his will observed in the minutest circumstances.

Ellicott traces Ithamar's appointment to his having been actively concerned in the construction of the tabernacle, and balances his oversight of the Gershonites and Merarites against the duties already assigned to Eleazar; he explains the naming by name from the heavier and more cumbersome parts falling to the Merarites, and prefers ye shall assign or appoint to ye shall reckon; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the charge in Ithamar's hand as carried out under his superintendence and parse the phrase for their charge as the things it was their business to bear.

debates: The age at which Levitical service began: the Hebrew has thirty, while the Greek version reads twenty-five both here and in the parallel place, agreeing with the rule given later in the book; Gill reconciles the two by treating twenty-five as the age of waiting and learning and thirty as the age of entry upon the work.

schools.summary: Calvin finds a further condition implied, that none were to be received who were not free from defect and blemish — the blind and lame having been excluded elsewhere lest their disfigurement produce contempt, and that they might be admonished by that sign to keep themselves the more diligently from all spiritual defilement — and observes that because the inequality of the charges might have bred envy, God's authority is asserted at the close, Moses recording that he acted only ministerially.

Henry reads the ratios: barely a third of the Kohathites and Gershonites were serviceable men, from which he concludes that of the many who add to the numbers of the church comparatively few contribute to the service of it; the Merarites, fewest in number but bearing the greatest burden, had more than half fit, since whatever service God calls men to he will furnish them for, giving strength in proportion to the work; and the whole Levitical muster of 8,580 is small beside the fighting tribes, because those who war after the flesh are always more than those who fight the good fight of faith.

Clarke sets the two censuses side by side in a table and exclaims at so many men all properly ecclesiastics, reckons the tabernacle's metal at nearly ten tons and fourteen hundred pounds besides the skins, hangings, cords, boards and posts, and lifts the structure into type — tabernacle and temple representing the Church and the humanity of Christ — before borrowing Ainsworth's fourfold parallel between the dismantling of the tabernacle and the death and resurrection of the body.
Keil and Delitzsch put the total of Levite males from a month old at 22,000 and remark that the 8,580 fit for service bears a just proportion to it.

debates: The size of the tribe as a whole: Clarke's table of the two censuses yields 22,300 Levites in all, of whom 13,720 were too old or too young, while Keil and Delitzsch reckon the males from a month old at 22,000.

44.pericope_label: The sum of the Levites fit for service

schools.summary: Gill devotes his last note to the two phrases in which the distribution is summed: the service of the ministry, or more literally a service of service, which Jarchi refers to the singing with cymbals and harps as one service performed towards another but which Gill thinks Chaskuni explains better of the taking down and setting up of the tabernacle, a duty lying on all the Levites alike; and the service of the burden, which Chaskuni restrains to the ark, table, candlestick and altars borne on Kohathite shoulders but which Gill would extend to whatever each man carried on the march — the whole done exactly as commanded, Moses attending to it punctually as a faithful servant in the house of God.

Wesley calls the disparity providential: where the burdens were fewer and easier only about a third proved fit for service, and where they were more numerous and heavier above half were fit, so that the strength was given where the weight was to be borne.
Ellicott observes that the 8,580 men between the ages named bear a just proportion to the 22,000 males of the tribe from a month old and upwards recorded in the earlier census.

debates: What the doubled phrase service of service means: Jarchi refers it to the Levites' singing with cymbals and harps, one service rendered towards another, while Chaskuni — whom Gill prefers — explains it of the taking down and setting up of the tabernacle, a duty incumbent on all the Levites.
